The study evaluated three different bypass ratio engines from both GE and Pratt & Whitney for integration with an advanced 777-sized aircraft.
The GE UEET engines utilized a dual, counter-rotating fan design while the P&W UEET engines incorporated a gearbox and variable area nozzle.
The optimal BPR was found to be 11 for the GE UEET engines and 14.3 for the P&W UEET engines.
The P&W UEET engines achieved better fuel efficiency improvement over the baseline PW4090 engine compared to the GE UEET engines over the GE90-94B.
The optimal P&W UEET powered airplane achieved approximately 2% better fuel efficiency than the best GE UEET powered airplane.
The heavier weight of the optimal P&W engine offset its fuel efficiency advantage, resulting in the same operating cost as the lighter GE engine.
A subcontract study by Tuskegee University found that the BPR versus block fuel efficiency trend held true for smaller and larger passenger aircraft.
The windmilling drag for the larger diameter P&W engines more than doubled at cruise Mach 0.8 conditions, which could impact ETOPS performance.
The study aimed for an 8-15% reduction in block fuel use, 70% reduction in LTO NOx emissions, and 20 dB cumulative noise reduction below Stage 3 limits.
The advanced study airplane used a composite wing with an aspect ratio of 10.2, compared to the metal wing with AR 8.7 on the baseline 777-200ER.
The advanced study airplane maintained the same 305 passenger capacity and 3,000 nmi mission range as the 777-200ER.
The advanced study airplane had to meet the same takeoff and landing field length performance as the baseline 777.
The GE engines showed an inverse relationship between fan pressure ratio and bypass ratio, with higher BPR engines having lower FPR.
The P&W engines demonstrated even higher BPR values than the GE engines at a given FPR, likely due to the gearbox technology.
The nacelle designs were modified by Boeing to achieve lower cruise and ETOPS drag compared to the initial P&W nacelle shapes.
